full_judgment: 7. The petitioner in his affidavit in-reply has not denied the fact of the institution of the aforesaid suit with pier for khas possession. As a matter of facts certified copy of the plaint of the said suit has been Annexed as Annexure 'C' to the affidavit-in-opposition which bears out the facts stated in the said affidavit. It is found that the said stilt includes the proceeding land as well which are plot Nos. 947 and 2387 under khatian No. 1143 within mouza Basrapur, P.S. Kotwali. It is abundantly clear from the plaint (annexure 'C') and the petition of the first party dated 6.9 82 (certified copy produced) that the first party was out of possession that only on the date of drawing up of the proceeding i.e. 29.3.83 but since long before that date i.e. 9.1.82 when T.S 12/82 was instituted. The first party having gone to the Civil Court long ago for recovery of khas possession of the proceeding land he cannot take the law into his own hand and try to create an "apprehension of breach of the peace" over the dispute and thus invoke the jurisdiction of the Magistrate under section 145 Cr.P.C. The learned Sessions Judge was justified in observing in the facts and circumstances of the case that the first party instituted the proceeding under section 145 Cr.PC. to recover, possession of the proceeding land, which power evidently, the Magistrate does not have under the said section. Being admittedly out of possession any alleged threat to peace over the dispute could only have been at the binding of the first party-petitioner himself. Upon the general principle of law a person cannot be allowed to take advantage of his own wrong. It is well settled that when a person is admittedly out of possession of the disputed land except as in proviso to sub-section (4) he cannot invoke the jurisdiction of the Magistrate under section 145 Cr.PC. on the alleged ground of apprehension of breach of the peace. It is not difficult to see through the game or gamble of the 1st party-petitioner as he filed his petition to the A.D.M. who was also a member of the Martial Law Complaint Cell. Evidently, he wanted to make a short circuit of the process of law in obtaining possession or dispossessing the second party of the land through the opportunities of time and occasion throwing to the winds his allegiance to the common law which is deplorable. Thus I am satisfied that in the facts of the case the proceeding at the instance of the first party petitioner was wholly misconceived and in such view of the matter the arguments of the learned Advocate for the petitioner are irrelevant.
